title: A Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP)
summary: Defines the Simple Network Management Protocol, a simple way to inspect or change management information on a network element from a remote location. It is a re-release of RFC 1098 with a changed status section. It was a standards-track document and is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: Network devices have settings and counters. This is a simple way to ask a device what is going on, or to tell it to change a setting, using short messages.

questions: what udp ports does snmp use
subtitle: The original SNMP: read and write the dials on a network device with simple get, set and trap messages carried in single UDP datagrams.

tldr.problem: Operators needed a simple, uniform way to inspect and change management information on hosts, gateways and other network elements from a remote station, without building complex logic into every device.
tldr.mechanism: Management is modeled as reading and writing variables. A manager sends a GetRequest, GetNextRequest or SetRequest, the agent replies with a GetResponse, and the agent can also send unsolicited traps. Every message is one UDP datagram.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1157 defined the first widely deployed SNMP. It is now Historic, and later work replaced this framework while keeping the basic get, set and trap model.

facts.label: Access modes
facts.value: READ-ONLY or READ-WRITE within a community

today: RFC 1157 has Historic status and obsoletes RFC 1098 as a re-release of it. Later work, including the Internet-standard management framework described in RFC 3410, superseded this version, though the get, set and trap model it introduced is still the shape of network management protocols.

sections.title: Background and Goals
sections.content:
RFC 1157 is a re-release of RFC 1098 with a changed status section and a few typographical corrections. It defines the Simple Network Management Protocol, a companion to the Structure of Management Information in RFC 1155 and the Management Information Base in RFC 1156. Together these describe how to name, model and exchange management information for TCP/IP internets.

The design deliberately minimizes the number and complexity of management functions inside the agent. That lowers the cost of building agents and leaves management tools free to be as elaborate as their makers want. The protocol is not backwardly compatible with its predecessor SGMP, and new UDP ports were allocated to avoid confusion with it.
sections.plainLanguage: The aim was to keep the part inside each device as small and simple as possible, so all the clever work happens at the manager's console.

sections.title: The SNMP Architecture
sections.content:
Management stations run applications that monitor and control network elements such as hosts, gateways and terminal servers. Each element hosts an agent that does the work. Because everything is modeled as inspecting or altering variables, an agent needs only two essential operations, get and set, and there are no imperative commands. A reboot, for instance, could be started by setting the parameter that counts seconds until restart.

Monitoring is mainly by polling, with a limited number of unsolicited traps used to guide timing and focus. Information is encoded in a subset of ASN.1 using only the definite-length form of the basic encoding rules, and only non-aggregate object types are covered. Access is organized into communities, each with a community name, a MIB view and an access mode of READ-ONLY or READ-WRITE. A proxy arrangement lets one agent manage devices that cannot speak the protocol themselves.
sections.plainLanguage: A manager polls devices with questions, and only a few urgent events make a device speak up on its own. A community name acts like a shared password word that says who is asking and what they may touch.

sections.title: Naming Object Instances
sections.content:
Each variable is named by an OBJECT IDENTIFIER of the form x.y, where x names an object type in the MIB and y identifies the instance. Object types with no special rule have their single instance at x.0, so sysDescr has its instance at the end of its type identifier followed by zero.

Table entries are named by their index, for example the type of interface 2 or the netmask of the interface with a given address. Related variables sit next to each other in lexicographic order, which is what makes the GetNextRequest operation useful for walking a table entry by entry.
sections.plainLanguage: Every setting in a device has a long numbered address, a bit like a shelf code in a library. Settings that belong together are shelved side by side, so you can read them one after another.

sections.title: Messages and Operations
sections.content:
A message contains a version identifier, a community name and a protocol data unit, carried as one UDP datagram. Agents receive ordinary messages on UDP port 161, while traps go to UDP port 162. An implementation need not accept messages longer than 484 octets, though larger datagrams are recommended where feasible, and all five PDU types are mandatory.

GetRequest retrieves named variables, GetNextRequest returns the next variable in lexicographic order and is how tables are traversed, and GetResponse carries the answer. SetRequest assigns values, and those assignments should take effect as if made simultaneously. A request identifier lets a manager match responses to outstanding requests and detect duplicates, which matters because UDP is unreliable. The error status field can report too big, no such name, bad value, read only or a general error, with the error index pointing at the variable at fault.
sections.plainLanguage: You can ask for a value, ask for the next one, set a value, receive an answer, or hear an alarm. Each message fits in one datagram, and a numbered ticket matches answers back to questions.

sections.title: Traps
sections.content:
A trap is an unsolicited report the agent sends without being asked. Its protocol data unit carries the enterprise object identifier, the sender address, a generic trap code, a specific trap code, a time stamp and variable bindings. The generic codes are cold start, warm start, link down, link up, authentication failure, EGP neighbor loss and enterprise specific.

Implementations must be able to generate the authentication failure trap but must also be able to suppress it through some implementation-specific mechanism. The link down and link up traps place the index of the affected interface first among their variable bindings, and the EGP neighbor loss trap does the same for the address of the affected neighbor.
sections.plainLanguage: A trap is the device ringing a bell without being asked: it just restarted, a cable came unplugged, or someone tried the wrong password.

sections.title: Authentication
sections.content:
The Security Considerations section states only that security issues are not discussed in this memo. The architecture does define an authentication service that decides whether a message is authentic for a given community, and the RFC notes that effective management requires services able to identify authentic messages with a high degree of certainty.

The community name travels in the clear and acts much like a password, so anyone who can read a datagram can learn it. The document also allows a trivial scheme in which every message is accepted as authentic, which leaves access controlled only by knowing a community name and reaching the device.
sections.plainLanguage: The rulebook mostly leaves the question of proving who is asking to other documents, and it permits a very trusting mode that believes everyone who knows the shared password word.

cells: Return the next variable in lexicographic order; used to walk tables.
Carry the answer, with error status and error index.
Report an event without being asked.

items.label: coldStart
items.desc: The sender is reinitializing and its configuration or implementation may change.

items.label: warmStart
items.desc: The sender is reinitializing without changing configuration or implementation.

items.label: linkDown
items.desc: A monitored communication link has failed.

items.label: linkUp
items.desc: A monitored communication link has come up.

items.label: authenticationFailure
items.desc: A received message was not properly authenticated.

items.label: egpNeighborLoss
items.desc: An EGP neighbor has been marked down.

items.label: enterpriseSpecific
items.desc: A vendor-defined event, named by the specific trap code.

items.title: Message contents
items.text: A version identifier, a community name and one protocol data unit.

items.title: Agent port
items.text: Ordinary messages are received on UDP port 161.

items.title: Trap port
items.text: Messages that report traps are received on UDP port 162.

items.title: Accepted size
items.text: An implementation need not accept messages longer than 484 octets.
